question.prompt:
Points \(R,\) \(S\) and \(T\) are vertices of an equilateral triangle, and points \(X,\) \(Y\) and \(Z\) are midpoints of its sides. How many noncongruent triangles can be drawn using any three of these six points as vertices?

[Figure 1](figures/2001_AMC_8_Q23_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
Triangles in different positions may still be congruent, so we will compare their three side lengths. Choose the unit so that each side of \(RST\) has length \(2\). As labeled, \(X,Y,Z\) are the midpoints of \(RT,RS,ST\), respectively. Each half-side has length \(1\), and the segments joining midpoints also have length \(1\).

We also need the distance from an original vertex to the opposite midpoint. In an equilateral triangle, that segment is perpendicular to the opposite side. The Pythagorean theorem therefore gives
\[
SX=\sqrt{2^2-1^2}=\sqrt3.
\]
The other two such distances have the same length.

Now classify a selection of three points by how many belong to \(R,S,T\).

• Three original vertices give \(RST\), with side lengths \((2,2,2)\).

• No original vertices give \(XYZ\), with side lengths \((1,1,1)\).

• Two original vertices can be taken as \(R,T\), since the other choices have the same geometry. Choosing \(X\) gives three collinear points, so it makes no triangle. Choosing either \(Y\) or \(Z\) gives side lengths \((1,\sqrt3,2)\).

• One original vertex can be taken as \(R\). The midpoint pair \(X,Y\) gives side lengths \((1,1,1)\). Either pair \(X,Z\) or \(Y,Z\) gives side lengths \((1,1,\sqrt3)\).

These cases include every selection. Triangles with the same three side lengths are congruent by SSS, while the four different triples cannot describe congruent triangles. Thus there are \(\boxed{4}\) noncongruent triangles, choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
solutions.title: Classify by the number of original vertices
